name: Autodesk Maya
tagline: Industry-standard 3D software for modeling, rigging, animation, simulation and rendering.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Maya is roughly three decades of accumulated numerical methods: deformers, skinning solvers, constraint graphs, nCloth, Bifrost, UV tooling, a node graph that production artists have memorized, and a plugin API that every studio pipeline hangs off. An agent can absolutely give you a mesh viewer with keyframes and a timeline in one session, and that is genuinely fun, but it is not the same category of object. The parts that matter are the ones that took specialists years each: a stable dual-quaternion skinning path, a robust UV unwrapper, a renderer that matches what the lighting lead expects. Even if you nailed the math, nobody else can open your scene file, and that alone ends the conversation for anything collaborative. Build a toy to learn the concepts, not to replace the tool.
coreLoopDIY: A local browser app that loads a mesh, lets you move objects and bones, set keyframes on a timeline, scrub playback, and export the animated result to glTF.
requirements: Sample glTF/GLB assets to load, since you are not building a modeler from scratch
whatYouLose: Real modeling tools: extrude, bevel, boolean, retopology, UV unwrapping, sculpting
Rigging that holds up: IK solvers, constraints, blend shapes, skin weight painting, deformers
Simulation: cloth, hair, fluids, rigid bodies, anything Bifrost touches
Production renderers (Arnold et al.) and the look-dev workflow around them
Interop: .ma/.mb files, USD and Alembic round trips, and every studio pipeline script written against the Maya API
moatNotes: The lock-in is partly file format and partly muscle memory. A rigger with ten years of Maya hotkeys and a shelf full of custom MEL is not migrating for a cheaper seat.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the people paying are usually billing clients, and the seat cost is noise against a day of artist time. Maya is what the pipeline, the freelancer you just hired, and the tutorial the junior is watching all assume. Blender is free and extremely good and has eaten real ground here, which tells you the moat is pipeline and institutional habit rather than raw capability, but in studios that habit is worth more than the license fee. Nobody buys Maya because the software is magic; they buy it because everyone downstream already speaks it.
notes: A keyframe timeline over a glTF scene is a weekend; a skinning solver that does not explode is not. The moat is thirty years of specialist numerical work plus every studio pipeline script written against the Maya API.
prompt:
Build a local 3D scene animator in the browser. This is a learning toy, not a Maya replacement, so scope it honestly.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Vite + TypeScript, no framework, plain DOM for the UI
- three.js for rendering and glTF loading
- Zustand for the scene/animation store
- No backend, no accounts, no telemetry, no network calls at runtime

In scope:
- Drag and drop a .glb or .gltf file onto the canvas to load it
- Viewport: orbit/pan/zoom camera, grid, a simple three-point light rig, toggle between shaded and wireframe
- Outliner panel listing the scene graph, click to select a node, selection highlighted with a bounding box helper
- Transform editing for the selected node: numeric inputs for position, rotation (euler, degrees) and scale, plus a translate/rotate gizmo via TransformControls
- Timeline panel: fixed 24 fps, adjustable frame range, a scrubbable playhead, play/pause/loop
- Keyframing: set a key on the selected node's current transform at the current frame, delete a key, keys drawn as diamonds on a per-node track row
- Interpolation between keys: linear and catmull-rom for position, slerp for rotation, chosen with a per-track dropdown
- Export: bake the animation into a glTF AnimationClip and download a .glb via GLTFExporter
- Save and load the whole project to a JSON file (scene node transforms plus keyframes) using the File System Access API with a download fallback
- Keyboard: space to play/pause, s to set key, arrow keys to step frames, f to frame selection

Explicitly out of scope, do not attempt, and put a short README section saying so:
- Any mesh editing, UV tools, sculpting, retopology
- Skinning, bone weight painting, IK, constraints, blend shapes
- Physics or any simulation
- Materials beyond what the imported glTF already carries
- Offline rendering or any output other than realtime WebGL and the .glb export

Quality bar: strict TypeScript, no any, render loop must hold 60 fps on a 100k triangle model, panels resizable, state survives a page reload via localStorage. Ship a README with run instructions and a one-paragraph list of everything real DCC software does that this does not.
